extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Spectator interested in literary taste, wit, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Short 18th-century periodical essays giving prescriptive guidance on wit, poetry, and social conduct (especially female behaviour and poetic taste). Includes critiques of 'false wit' and examples of bad poetic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper spheres of men and women
rubrics_metrics.description: Men and Women ought to busy themselves in their proper Spheres, and on such Matters only as are suitable to their respective Sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison invokes Homer (Hector/Andromache) to argue that each sex should confine itself to appropriate topics and activities. He gives examples of a young gentleman skilled in nursery arts and a rural woman who hunts and uses coarse language to show that actions indifferent in themselves appear ridiculous when coming from the 'wrong' sex. Anti-pattern: transplanting the faults and imperfections of one sex into another results in a 'black and monstrous' appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women should avoid party-zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing so bad for the Face as Party-Zeal; it gives an ill-natured Cast to the Eye, and a disagreeable Sourness to the Look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political/party fury spoils a woman's beauty and temper, produces strong lines, and hastens complexional decline; it makes conversation angry and extravagant. Addison advises female readers to abstain from such disputes to preserve amiability and appearance, while allowing elderly 'motherly Partizans' license because they pose less danger of spoiling beauty or gaining converts. Example/anti-pattern: 'Camilla' who values partisan virago-hood over being the toast of both sides, and who scalded her fingers in a heated debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for clarity: make wit intelligible to ordinary capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall endeavour to make what I say intelligible to ordinary Capacities; but if my Readers meet with any Paper that in some Parts of it may be a little out of their Reach, I would not have them discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers of wit and criticism should primarily address ordinary readers and avoid unnecessary obscurity; occasional difficult passages may be tolerated but overall accessibility is a goal. Addison promises a sequence that will be progressively clearer, implying a serial-critical approach to explicating difficult subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of criticism: banish vice and ignorance and establish polite taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The great and only End of these my Speculations is to banish Vice and Ignorance out of the Territories of Great-Britain, ... to establish among us a Taste of polite Writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be reformative and civic-minded: refine public taste (opera, tragedy, comedy) and improve manners through literary example. The critic's remit includes practical improvement of theatrical and poetic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true wit from false wit (avoid industry without genius)
rubrics_metrics.description: False Wit ... is where a Writer does not show himself a Man of a beautiful Genius, but of great Industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False wit is characterized by mechanical cleverness and laborious contrivance rather than genuine imagination. Critically, identify performances that prioritize artifice over substance. Addison will trace varieties of false wit and show how they masquerade as talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sacrifice sense to shape in 'picture' or shaped poems
rubrics_metrics.description: The Author seems to have been more intent upon the Figure of his Poem, than upon the Sense of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape-poems (egg, wings, ax, altar, etc.) that force verse length and diction to fit a visual outline are condemned when form is preferred to meaning. Anti-pattern: stretching or chopping lines (Procrustes analogy) to make them fit the mould, producing cramped or mutilated poetry. Example: shaped verses of the ancients and modern revivals are suspect when sense is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lipogrammatic artifices as literary merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Lipogrammiatists or Letter-droppers ... would take an Exception ... so as not to admit [a particular letter] once into a whole Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremely constrained experiments (omitting letters) create obsolete words, barbarisms, rude spellings, and a corpus of oddities rather than genuine poetry. Anti-pattern: an 'Odyssey' constructed by systematically banishing letters produces a treasury of obsolescences rather than lasting art; such feats are examples of false wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with rebuses and pictorial substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rebus ... substitutes a Picture in [place] of a Word. Sometimes used for concealment or cleverness, it can look like a pun in an heroic context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically used (Cæsar's elephant, Cicero's vetch) for lawful or witty effect, but in grand monuments or noble architecture such devices often reduce the work to a 'pun' or poor conceit. Example/anti-pattern: Blenheim's carved device of a lion tearing a cock appears like a pun and blemishes an otherwise noble design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making echoes speak rationally or supply rhymes (a silly conceit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Conceit of making an Eccho talk sensibly, and give rational Answers ... is an example of a false kind of Wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personifying an echo to answer in learned languages or to help a poet with rhymes is ludicrous rather than witty. Examples: Erasmus's dialogue with a polyglot Echo and Hudibras's ridicule of Echo providing rhymes illustrate this device's absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match inventive devices to appropriate poetic forms (Pindaric suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: I would humbly propose ... that admirable English Authors who call themselves Pindarick Writers, that they would apply themselves to this kind of Wit ... as being provided better than any other Poets with Verses of all Sizes and Dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing playful or shaped devices, prefer forms (e.g., pindaric/irregular verse) naturally suited to variable line lengths and sizes. This is a conditional endorsement: inventive visual or metric experiments are acceptable when aligned with a form's structural flexibility; anti-pattern is forcing such devices into rigid forms (heroic couplet) where they become deformed.
